items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover why snake embryos twist into spirals
items.content_html: Snake embryos begin life curled into a distinctive right-handed spiral, and scientists may finally know why. Their bodies grow faster than their guts, creating a tether that forces the lengthening embryo to buckle and twist inside the egg. Researchers reached the conclusion after studying more than 900 embryos and using CT scans to reveal the hidden anatomy behind the coils.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A massive plume deep beneath Africa is pulling the continent apart
items.content_html: A vast plume rising from deep inside Earth may be responsible for mysterious movements along the East African Rift. The discovery reveals how forces deep in the mantle are working alongside shallower geological forces as the continent slowly pulls apart.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists find a human-only gene that may help explain our brainpower
items.content_html: Scientists discovered that human microglia, immune cells that help shape developing brain circuits, can take four to eight years to mature instead of just weeks as they do in mice. The unusually slow process may help explain how the human brain develops its remarkable complexity and cognitive abilities.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] High blood sugar may help cancer cells hide from the immune system
items.content_html:
🔧 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Researchers discovered a possible way cancer cells hide from the immune system: they build a thick, sugar-rich coating around themselves. High blood sugar can strengthen this protective shield under conditions that resemble the environment inside tumors, with the protein HSF1 playing a key role. Blocking this process could make cancer cells easier for the immune system to recognize and destroy.

items.content_html:

Methanol poisoning from contaminated alcohol is relatively rare in countries with strict alcohol regulation, but it remains a serious problem in regions where counterfeit alcohol is common. Outbreaks continue to occur every year, causing deaths, blindness, and permanent injuries. A few years ago in Laos, six foreign tourists died after drinking at a backpacker hostel, and an even bigger outbreak occurred in Turkey in 2025, taking the lives of 160 people and leaving more than 250 incapacitated. Both cases were attributed to methanol poisoning from illegally produced alcohol.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A “quantum bath” puts quantum entanglement on autopilot
items.content_html: Physicists have demonstrated a new way to entangle distant quantum bits without the constant measurements and active control normally required. The team created a “quantum bath,” a shared environment filled with correlated microwave photons that automatically pushes separated qubits into an entangled state and helps keep them there. The experiment confirms a theoretical prediction made more than 20 years ago and could offer a simpler way to connect modules in future quantum computers.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth
items.content_html: A long-standing picture of brain evolution as newer, rational layers stacked on top of an ancient “lizard brain” may be deeply misleading. Researchers found that evolution instead appears to balance two competing styles of brain wiring, expanding one while shrinking the other depending on what an animal needs to survive.

items.title: [dhakatribune.com] NASA launches Roman telescope to map hidden universe
items.content_html:
🎨 🌲 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌲 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌲 🔭 ✏️

NASA launched the $4.3 billion Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope at 7:26 a.m. EDT Sunday on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida [nasa.gov#2][pbs.org#1][npr.org#1]. NASA said ground controllers at Goddard Space Flight Center began receiving telemetry seven minutes after liftoff, and Roman separated from the rocket 31 minutes into the flight [nasa.gov#2]. Roman began a roughly three-month journey of about 1 million miles to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point, where it will operate near the James Webb Space Telescope [nasa.gov#2][sci.news#1][pbs.org#1]. NASA describes Roman as a flagship mission built to study dark matter, dark energy and exoplanets through wide-field infrared surveys that cover large areas of sky with Hubble-like sharpness [nasa.gov#2][scientificamerican.com#1][bbc.co.uk#1]. NASA plans a five-year mission and says the telescope may carry enough fuel for five additional years [tribune.com.pk#1][ksl.com#1]. Roman is named for Nancy Grace Roman, NASA’s first chief of astronomy, who is widely associated with the development of the Hubble Space Telescope [eos.org#1][sci.news#1][discovermagazine.com#4].

items.title: [ScienceDaily] IBM quantum computer solves classically intractable problem in 15 minutes
items.content_html: IBM and University of Chicago researchers have completed a quantum computation that leading classical methods could not practically reproduce. The system used 70 error-corrected logical qubits and finished the task in roughly 15 minutes while also providing statistical evidence that the result was reliable.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Hundreds of hidden earthquakes found at Antarctica’s Doomsday Glacier
items.content_html: Hundreds of previously overlooked seismic events have been detected beneath Antarctica, including 245 near the marine edge of the Thwaites Glacier. Many appear to be glacial earthquakes caused when huge icebergs break off, capsize, and collide with the glacier. The surge in activity coincided with a period when Thwaites was flowing faster toward the ocean, hinting that changing ocean conditions may be destabilizing the ice.

items.title: [benchmark.pl] NASA sets Roman telescope launch for August 30
items.content_html: NASA plans to launch the $4.3 billion Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on August 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, with liftoff set for 7:26 a.m. ET [space.com#2][satellitetoday.com#1][ft.com#1]. The observatory is designed to study dark energy, dark matter, exoplanets and infrared astrophysics after traveling to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point, about 1 million miles, or 1.5 million kilometers, from Earth [scitechdaily.com#1][earthsky.org#1][infobae.com#1][indiatoday.in#1]. Roman carries a 2.4-meter primary mirror, the same diameter as Hubble's. Its Wide Field Instrument can image an area at least 100 times larger than Hubble's cameras while retaining Hubble-like sharpness [sciencedaily.com#1][theconversation.com#1][newscientist.com#1][spacedaily.com#1]. NASA and scientists involved in the mission say that combination will let Roman survey large regions of the sky, measure light from up to a billion galaxies and search for large numbers of planets beyond the solar system [pbs.org#1][popsci.com#1][infobae.com#1]. The telescope has an unusual origin: The National Reconnaissance Office transferred unused telescope hardware to NASA in 2012 after optical components originally developed for a reconnaissance program were left in storage [pbs.org#1][spacedaily.com#1][benchmark.pl#1][wp.pl#1]. NASA then spent more than a decade converting the inherited hardware into a civilian astrophysics observatory with new instruments, spacecraft systems and deep-space mission requirements [spacedaily.com#1][benchmark.pl#1][scitechdaily.com#1].
